title: AI Data Centers Look Beyond Just GPUs
gist: A six-way industry roundtable (Arm, Axiomise, Cadence, Expedera, Siemens EDA, Synopsys) argues the AI data center is splitting the inference pipeline into separate prefill, decode and agent-execution clusters, each with its own hardware/software mix, ending the one-GPU-solves-everything era. The binding constraints are shifting from FLOPs to interconnect topology, HBM utilization and the orchestration software that must span multi-vendor heterogeneous fleets.

themes.theme: Inference disaggregation as the new architecture

insights.claim: Inference is being physically disaggregated into separate clusters for prefill, decode and agent tool-execution, each with a different hardware and software mix, stitched together most likely over Ethernet today.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: If clusters specialize by inference stage, demand splits into distinct silicon TAMs; a vendor strong only in matrix math captures a shrinking share of the rack.
insights.quote: you have a cluster with a specific set of hardware and software to do the pre-filled stage, then you have a cluster to do the decode stage, and then you have another fully compute cluster to do the execution by the agents
insights.locator: What we are seeing with inference disaggregated

insights.claim: Arm's cloud and AI infrastructure silicon lead frames the prefill stage as extremely compute-intensive and distinct enough that a non-GPU processor is being deployed specifically for it, citing an LPU (Language Processing Unit) announced for prefill clusters.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Purpose-built prefill silicon is the first commercially visible crack in GPU universality; watch which vendors claim that stage.
insights.quote: Recently, Nvidia announced its Groq 3 LPU (Language Processing Unit) to be used in the prefill cluster, showing that more than a GPU is required to do some of these tasks.
insights.locator: Bhattacharjee: That's right. One of the trends

insights.claim: The panel's explicit thesis is that the industry has recognized the GPU is not the right tool for every AI task, with inference having 'completely different workload characteristics' from the math-heavy training work GPUs were optimized for.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: A stated end to GPU monoculture from an Arm executive is a directional signal for accelerator diversification budgets at hyperscalers.
insights.quote: The industry is recognizing that every nail doesn’t have one hammer, which is the GPU.
insights.locator: So there’s a need to get more diverse hardware

insights.claim: Reasoning workloads should be assigned to 'accelerators' rather than GPUs specifically, with custom ASICs explicitly named as valid substitutes for the matrix-multiplication role.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Deliberate vocabulary shift from GPU to accelerator inside a chip-IP vendor is a tell that ASIC substitution is being planned for, not merely theorized.
insights.quote: I’ll use the word accelerators instead of GPU, because it doesn’t have to be a GPU. It can be a custom ASIC, which is doing the reasoning function.
insights.locator: That’s where the accelerators come in

insights.claim: Agentic orchestration and tool calling are asserted to run on CPUs rather than accelerators, giving the CPU a defined and growing role in AI inference rather than a diminishing one.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Agent-heavy workloads add server CPU demand per accelerator, supporting CPU attach-rate stories that the GPU narrative has overshadowed.
insights.quote: But when it comes to orchestration tool calling, which is basically agents taking their actions, those can all run on CPU.
insights.locator: Bhattacharjee: If you think about inference, there’s a reasoning part

insights.claim: NVLink is described as the de facto industry standard for accelerator-to-accelerator connection but works only within the Nvidia ecosystem, which is the stated reason hyperscalers are building their own accelerators and their own interconnects.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Interconnect lock-in is named as the direct cause of custom-silicon programs; erosion of that lock-in is the key variable for Nvidia's share of the rack.
insights.quote: That’s where Nvidia came up with NVLink, which is kind of the industry standard. But it only works with the Nvidia ecosystem. This is why the hyperscalers are all creating their own accelerators.
insights.locator: So for the accelerator-to-accelerator connection

insights.claim: NVLink Fusion is characterized as a partial opening in which Nvidia must remain on one side of every link — either its accelerator or its CPU — so the 'open' standard still guarantees Nvidia content in the system.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Read NVLink Fusion as a moat-preservation move, not genuine openness; it caps how much Nvidia silicon can be designed out of a Fusion-based rack.
insights.quote: So Nvidia came up with NVLink Fusion, where Nvidia needs to be on one side of the equation.
insights.locator: There’s pressure on Nvidia, as well, to open up NVLink

insights.claim: UALink, backed by a consortium with AMD's Instinct line explicitly cited as a beneficiary, is positioned as the standards counterweight to NVLink for accelerator-to-accelerator links.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: UALink adoption is the cleanest observable proxy for whether merchant accelerators can win scale-up sockets against Nvidia.
insights.quote: There is also a consortium called UA, and they’re coming up with UALink (Ultra Accelerator Link) to connect the accelerators together.
insights.locator: In that case, NVLink Fusion works

insights.claim: A one-to-two-year timeline is given for both accelerator-to-accelerator and host-to-accelerator interconnects to become standardized, driven by hyperscaler demand rather than by chip vendors.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: A dated convergence forecast gives a window to watch: standardized links by roughly 2027-2028 would compress proprietary-interconnect pricing power.
insights.quote: So if you fast forward maybe a year or two, this is going to be more standardized, where there will be adoption from the hyperscalers, which are the ones driving it
insights.locator: There is also a consortium called UA

insights.claim: Google's TPU fleet is stitched together with an optical Interchip Interconnect (ICI) that is entirely Google-specific, an approach the Arm executive credits as well-executed but non-transferable.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Optical interchip links at hyperscaler scale validate silicon-photonics demand while showing bespoke fabrics remain a moat, not a merchant product.
insights.quote: Google created the TPU, and they have their own way of connecting TPUs together using optical interconnect, which they call ICI (Interchip Interconnect).
insights.locator: This is why the hyperscalers are all creating their own accelerators

insights.claim: Amazon Trainium, Meta's MTIA and Microsoft's Maia are named as all now needing the same accelerator-interconnect capability, and none of them want to solve the problem individually — the structural driver pushing the market toward a standard.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Three more hyperscaler accelerator programs needing a shared fabric is the demand base that makes UALink-style standards commercially viable.
insights.quote: Now, if you look at Amazon with their training, and Meta with their MTIA (Meta Training and Inference Accelerator), and Microsoft with their own Maia, all of these guys need similar capabilities now.
insights.locator: Google has done a good job in terms of creating a whole different way

themes.theme: Memory and parallelism dictate cluster topology

insights.claim: Expedera's chief scientist argues memory — specifically the cost and utilization of HBM — became the critical bottleneck for GPUs as model sizes grew, displacing raw compute as the design constraint.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: HBM utilization efficiency, not just HBM supply, is the margin lever; architectures that raise effective HBM use erode the volume needed per deployment.
insights.quote: given how the models have increased in size, the memory became one of the critical bottlenecks that needed to be utilized with the computations. That’s where the cost of HBM and how the HBM is utilized become very important factors for GPUs
insights.locator: Chole: A lot of it has to do with the workload

insights.claim: Model memory is split into a static parameter component and a dynamic context component, and it is the dynamic context — scaled by concurrent requests per second — that determines data center memory sizing rather than model weights alone.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Memory demand scales with concurrency and context length, not parameter count — a much steeper curve that supports sustained HBM/high-bandwidth memory demand.
insights.quote: While you have the parameters that are like a static part of the models, there is a dynamic part of the model, which is the context.
insights.locator: Chole: A lot of it has to do with the workload

insights.claim: Each parallelization paradigm — tensor, data, context and pipeline parallel — imposes a different network topology requirement, with pipeline parallel being point-to-point while tensor parallel demands all-reduce and broadcast, meaning cluster design must be chosen against the intended parallelism strategy up front.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Topology is workload-specific, so 'GPU count' is a poor proxy for capability; interconnect fit determines realized throughput and thus true capex efficiency.
insights.quote: you basically end up going into different parallelization paradigms, such as tensor parallel, data parallel, context parallel, pipeline parallel, and with each there is a different requirement about topology
insights.locator: So when you put this whole thing together

insights.claim: Achieving anything close to 8x performance when scaling from one GPU to eight is described as a persistent unsolved challenge, undercutting linear-scaling assumptions embedded in cluster capex plans.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Sub-linear scaling means headline cluster FLOPs overstate delivered capacity; interconnect and software vendors monetize the gap.
insights.quote: How you go from one GPU to eight GPUs and still get close to 8X performance is always a challenge.
insights.locator: If there is enough API usage for your workload

themes.theme: Software and orchestration as the real bottleneck

insights.claim: Because heterogeneous cluster hardware will come from different companies, the software layer that seamlessly assigns work across mixed vendors is identified as a 'huge software challenge' and the gating factor on the whole disaggregated architecture.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Whoever owns cross-vendor scheduling captures the value that CUDA captured in the single-vendor era; a key place to look for the next software moat.
insights.quote: There’s a huge software challenge associated with this, because most of this hardware will come from different companies.
insights.locator: It’s called a heterogeneous cluster, if you will

insights.claim: Agentic workloads convert AI serving into a cloud-management problem in which the MCP (Model Context Protocol) server must be deployed and responsive and tool applications provisioned, meaning inference infrastructure now inherits classic distributed-systems operations risk.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Agent serving costs include orchestration and tool-runtime overhead outside the accelerator; models of token economics that ignore this understate cost.
insights.quote: the agentic workload becomes more like a cloud management problem, where the tool applications have to be provided, and the MCP (Model Context Protocol) server has to be responsive and deployed
insights.locator: For example, if it’s a completely agentic workflow

insights.claim: Siemens EDA's HPC lead says hyperscalers already expose 'placement group' primitives that co-locate VMs on high-speed interconnect, and that performance collapses once a workload spans machines — making software placement, not hardware count, the determinant of scaling.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Off-machine hops are the scaling cliff; rack-scale integration that keeps workloads on one high-speed domain is where premium pricing is justified.
insights.quote: When you go off of one machine, this is a big problem if you want to try to get that linear kind of scaling as you add more machines to your app.
insights.locator: Brunner: We see the hardware vendors and large systems integrators

insights.claim: NeoCloud providers are cited as early adopters of heterogeneous inference, with DigitalOcean specifically deploying a five-layer inference architecture tuned for mixed AMD and Nvidia hardware and signaling more vendors to come.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Second-tier clouds differentiating on multi-vendor inference stacks is the demand channel that gives non-Nvidia accelerators real deployment volume.
insights.quote: DigitalOcean announced the deployment of a five-layer architecture for inference, specifically tuned toward using heterogeneous clusters underneath, with mention of AMD and Nvidia.
insights.locator: The NeoCloud companies are involved here

insights.claim: The explicit motive for heterogeneous clusters is stated as reducing the cost of tokens, tying architectural fragmentation directly to unit-economics pressure on inference providers.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Token cost is the forcing function; any vendor that cannot demonstrably lower cost per token loses the architectural argument regardless of peak specs.
insights.quote: That’s the trend to bring out the efficiency and reduce the cost of the tokens.
insights.locator: They said there will be new hardware incorporated, as well

insights.claim: Siemens EDA is already planning to integrate quantum machines into the same commonly connected cluster platform alongside conventional accelerators, treating quantum as another heterogeneous element rather than a separate facility.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Quantum entering the mainstream cluster-integration conversation from an EDA vendor is an early-cycle signal worth tracking for tooling and interconnect suppliers.
insights.quote: in our environment, we’re also looking at integrating quantum machines, which will be awesome. And that’s a whole kind of different way of feeding those and keeping those integrated.
insights.locator: Brunner: Heterogeneity inside of clusters

insights.claim: The panel treats Alibaba's 10,000-card compute cluster as a legitimate architectural workaround for lacking access to the latest Nvidia chips, with network design plus software workload placement compensating for weaker per-card silicon.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: Scale-out plus smart placement partially substitutes for banned leading-edge parts, weakening the assumption that export controls cleanly cap Chinese AI capacity.
insights.quote: Alibaba said it developed a 10,000-card compute cluster for a data center, which may be a workaround for not having the latest Nvidia chips.
insights.locator: SE: Alibaba said it developed a 10,000-card compute cluster
